Executive Summary
The United Nations Common Country Strategic Framework (UNCCSF) is the result of an 
internal consultative process launched by the Office of the UN Resident Coordinator in 2010 
to analyze how the United Nations Country Team (UNCT) can most effectively coordinate its 
activities in response to Saudi Arabia‟s national priorities and needs. While a formal UN 
Development Assistance Framework (UNDAF) is not mandatory for Saudi Arabia as a UN 
non-harmonized country context, the CCSF is intended to set the strategic vision and 
direction for UNCT work in coming years and serve as an easily accessible overview, 
internally and externally, of the UNs general goals and activities in the Kingdom. 
The coming years will be defined by important contextual changes for the UN-Saudi Arabia 
partnership: globally in the emergence of the post-2015 development agenda, regionally 
through the systemic changes in the Arab region following events in 2011, and nationally as a 
result of emerging development challenges. 
The CCSF is guided by an analysis of some of these trendsas encapsulated in a UN Common 
Country Analysis (CCA) undertaken by the UNCT in 2010-2011, the goals and targets of the 
Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), and Saudi Arabia‟sNinth National Development 
Plan (2010-2014) and related national strategies and policies. Five inter-related areas of focus 
for UN cooperation have been identified: 
(1) Effective and Accountable Governance: Enhanced participation, accountability, 
transparency, and justice.
(2) Inclusive Growth and Employment:Expanding non-oil growth opportunities and 
addressing those marginalized in the workforce - youth, women and migrant workers
(3) Social Protection and Services: Enhanced quality of education, health, social services.
(4) Sustainability of Natural Resources and Environment: Expanding energy efficiency, 
green economy approaches, mitigating climate change, and water conservation.
(5) Global Partnerships and South-South Cooperation:Enhanced linkages between UN 
initiatives and Saudi Arabia‟s growing global role on development and humanitarian issues.
Across all five pillars, crosscutting issues of capacity development, human rights (including 
labour rights), women‟s empowerment, and youth and adolescents are mainstreamed. 
The UNCTbring comparative advantages under all five areas with regard to achieving further 
tangible progress toward the goals of the 9
th National Development Plan and the Millennium 
Development Goals (MDGs),its values; global knowledge networks, best practices and 
lessons learned;and its impartialitybased on a track record of almost 70 years of presence and 
development cooperation within the Kingdom providing technical assistance to design 
effective national strategies and policies.4
I. Introduction
Saudi Arabia achieveda ranking of 0.77 on the UN‟s Human Development Index (HDI) in 
2011, placing it in the high HDI category and ranked 56 out of 187 countries. As noted in the 
2011 National Millennium Development Goal (MDG) Report, the Kingdom is on track to 
achieve most of the MDGs by 2015, and has made great strides on economic competitiveness 
rankings as well. Related to MDG 8, the Kingdom has also emerged as a strong supporter of 
global development partnerships, now standing as one of the largest providers of ODA to 
global development and humanitarian efforts. 
Despite its rise in various rankings such as HDI and economic competitiveness, the Kingdom 
faces several challenges looking to the future. Globally the world continues to face financial 
difficulties owing to the crisis in the West, while new drivers of global growth are emerging 
across the emerging South. Related to this is also the emergence of the post-2015 
development agenda, with a new paradigm and framework for development set to take shape 
by 2015. Regionally,countries have seen a historic period of systemic change in the Arab 
region following series of citizen-led revolutions in 2011. This has implications for Saudi 
Arabia both in terms of its role in the region as well as various dynamics of change locally. 
Nationally several important challenges are emerging calling for well targeting development 
policies. 
Citizen calls for more transparent, accountable and participatory governance are on the rise, 
as are concerns for more inclusive development taking into account the empowerment of 
vulnerable groups like religious minorities, women and migrant workers. While progress in 
governance capacities have been noted in recent years, important challenges remain, 
particularly with regard to issues of transparency, accountability and participation, and rightsbased approaches to development. An increasingly vocal and social media savvy youth are 
engaged in greater public participation and debates over the future of development. To 
engage these trends a series of new measures to enhance transparency, accountability and 
participation a being pursued. This includes enhanced local governance monitoring and 
effectiveness, at the frontline of development. In 2011, the Kingdom held it‟s second ever 
municipal elections and passed a new women vote policy whereby women would be able to 
stand as candidates for and vote in the next municipal elections, set for 2015. 
Building on its membership in the UN Human Rights Council 2011-12 term, Saudi Arabia is 
also planning measures to improve the situation of vulnerable groups within the country, 
including religious minorities, women and foreign workers. Along with other Gulf countries 
the Kingdom provided a constructive role in 2011 passage of the new UN Convention on 
Domestic Workers while in 2012 Saudi Arabia issued new draft legislation which if passed in 
coming years could see an end to the individual sponsorship and passport control systems for
migrant workers. New legislation tocombat human trafficking has also been issued in recent 
years with a need for effective implementation capacities. 
From an economic perspective, issues of youth unemployment also top the agenda of 
emerging development issues. The structure of economic growth has exacerbated both 
income and non-income inequalities among the local population with serious gaps between 
regions and strata of society. Past development results have largely based on oil-export 
revenues, with modest progress on diversification of the economy and employment 5
generation for a large and growing youth population. Todayupto 90% of public revenues still 
derived from oil export revenues. Saudi youth face30% unemployment and are often resigned 
to public sector posts, while expatriates enjoy 90% of all jobs within a dynamic and growing 
private sector, with most earnings repatriated abroad. The quota based affirmative action 
policies of the past (termed „Saudization‟) have had challenges in increasing the share of 
locals in the workforce. New efforts at growth-oriented employment creation and human 
capacity development are in focus,so the 60% of the country that makeup the youth can 
effectively compete with expatriates and more fully participate in global and national 
economic prosperity.
The institutional and human development capacities to address the growing challengesof
sustainable and inclusive growth remain low relative to other high income countries. A 
serious mismatch exists between youth skills and emerging employment opportunities,
especially among females.Women empowerment has thuscame into particular attention, 
boosted by an increasingly vocal and active women empowerment social movement among 
youth. Youth employment requires accelerated creation of knowledge-based jobs in 
particular. While a series of new universities have arisen in recent times to continue the 
process of expanding access to higher education, serious challenges exists in preparing youth 
through equally effective primary and secondary education systems. Overcoming a continued 
lack of opportunities for this overwhelmingly young population is necessary to underpin 
long-term sustainable development of Saudi society. The process of drafting a National 
Youth Strategy and launching a series of new youth oriented foundations and NGOs are an 
important step in this process, with a need to develop the capacities of these new systems and 
institutions to achieve national goals of inclusive and sustainable growth. 
Issues of natural resources use and environmental sustainability are also in focus. In 2011 the 
Kingdom completed its Second National Communication to the UNon Climate Change 
highlighting the serious challenges from rising energy intensity of growth, alongside 
increased vulnerabilities from growing scarcity of arable land and naturally available 
freshwater. With most power still producedby oil-burning facilities, the Kingdom‟s local oil 
consumption has grown steadily andnow outpaces GDP growth. This causes concern among 
some Government entities as to the future of the oil-export based development model, and the 
lost opportunity of future export revenues which have thus far served as the foundation of the 
country‟s human development results. Thus great attention and new policies are being issued 
with regards energy efficiency and renewable energy which are critical to sustaining 
development. Water resource scarcity is also of concern, with groundwater resources under 
pressure from growing industrial uses, pollution loads and rapid urbanization, all exacerbated 
by climate change trends. The latter has also been cause of concern in coastal areas in recent 
times, with major flood crises experienced along the Red Sea coast in 2011. Public awareness 
of energy and environmental sustainability will also need to be addressed simultaneously to
improving livelihoods and economic conditions.
Lastly, while seeking to address various local development challenges, the Kingdom has also 
increased its attention to helping address various global development priorities, now standing 
as one of the largest providers of ODA to global development and humanitarian efforts. This 
includes important large financial support to UN humanitarian efforts in crisis contexts such 
as Haiti, Pakistan and Somalia in recent years. In particular, South-South cooperation offers 
considerable scope for Saudi Arabia to engage developing countries around the world and to 
support the international public goods agenda. In so doing, it can promote activities that 
generate a “double dividend” by stimulating technical and institutional capacities and other 6
beneficial effects both within the Kingdom and abroad. Saudi Arabia is strongly positioned 
political and economically as the largest economy in the Arab region, holding a lead role in a 
number of multilateral process and institutions including OPEC, the G20, the Islamic 
Development Bank, and playing an important role in various UN fora including membership 
in the UN Human Rights Council in 2011-12. 
II. CCSF Vision
Beyond financial assets, economic, social and natural capitals are the keys to prosperity and 
represent the real wealth of nations. As the Kingdom moves forward in implementing the 9th
National Development Plan, it has allocated a record $386 billion in coming years to help 
build the pillars for broader inclusive, sustainable prosperity of its people. A series of well 
targeted development policies and institutions are needed to achieve this goal. It is toward 
this goal that the United Nations in Saudi Arabia will work, building not only the economy‟s 
tangible assets, but also the country‟s social and natural capital, including values of human 
rights, equity, cultural integrity and ecological balance. In particular, the UNCT can help to 
expand national innovation towards these goals by ensuring stronger inter-linkages among 
local and global partners, and various segments of society – public agencies, private 
enterprises, universities, and civil society organizations – to create and apply knowledge and 
capacities. 
To these ends, the United Nations Country Team (UNCT),1through a process of internal 
consultationsamong UNCT members, and between the Office of the UN Resident 
Coordinator and the Government, has prepared this UN Common Country Strategic 
Framework (CCSF) as a basis for increased collaboration, coherence and effectiveness of UN 
resident and non-residentagency activitiesin the period 2012-2016. It represents an internal 
coordination instrument to facilitate the development of partnerships among agencies and 
explore potential areas of UN activity between the UN and national partners. It seeks to 
reflect the aspirations of not only the MDGs and the National Development Plan, but also the 
rights-based commitments of the Millennium Declaration and international norms, 
Conventions and human rights instruments. 
The CCSF embodies a collective, coherent and integrated response by the UN to national 
priorities and guiding principles as set out in Saudi Arabia‟s Ninth National Development 
Plan (NDP) with its six overarching goals: improving standards of living, regional 
development, economic diversification, knowledge-based economy and competitiveness, and 
human resources including youth and women. Enhanced UN cooperation in the 
Kingdombrings access to a global network of expertise and builds on success cooperation and 
presence in the Kingdom for almost 70 years. 
CCSF Working Groups were established for each pillar, chaired by UNCT members, playing 
a lead role in CCSF preparations as information exchange and discussion platform and
further refining draft outcomes and indicators. At the same time, the CSSF is not a UNDAF 
and thus is a voluntary process; a living document flexible enough to respond to Saudi 
Arabia‟s evolving political, social and economic context and the evolving strategic directions 
 
1
The United Nations is represented in Saudi Arabia by UNDP, UNICEF, UNHCR, FAO and WHO, as well as 
the World Bank/IFC. Non-resident Agencies include ESCWA, UNESCO, ILO, UNEP, UNIDO, UNFPA, 
OHCHR, OCHA, IAEA, UN Women, UN HABITAT and UNIC. 7
of the UN system in coming years. TheCCSF also benefited from non-resident United 
Nations Agencies, as well as inputs from Government for quality support and assurance 
before being finalized. Individual UN agencies are expected to align their County Programme 
Documents for the period 2012-2016 in a manner that supports and reinforces the common 
vision expressed in the CCSF. 
The CCSF is intended to actively support national priorities; be better targeted and focused; 
be achievable and inspiring; and, above all, have impact. Overall, the United Nations goal is 
swift convergence in inter-agency planning – designing certain interventions collaboratively 
and sharing these as an integrated whole, allowing the United Nations to be an active, wellcoordinated and responsive partner with the people and Government of Saudi Arabia.
III. CCSFResults
The CCSF focuses on fivekey results, based on the UN Country Analysis (2011) of key 
development issues in the Kingdom, outcomes of UN internal reviews and a UNCT Strategic 
Planning Retreat in 2011 and advice and inputs in 2011-12 from the Regional UN 
Development Group (Regional UNDG). The five results are:
 Effective and Accountable Governance
 Inclusive Growth and Employment
 Social Protection and Services
 Sustainability of Natural Resources and Environment
 Global Partnerships and South-South Cooperation
The priority areas are complemented by four equally important crosscutting themes to further 
underpin interventions in all five pillars: capacity development; human rights (including 
labour rights); women‟s empowerment; and youth and adolescents. Selection of common 
issues was determined by the following criteria: alignment with national priorities, magnitude 
of the issue for development trends, impact on social cohesion and regional disparities; and 
comparative advantage of the UN system in addressing the challenges drawing on our 
neutrality, normative mandate, and global knowledge base.
The United Nations in Saudi Arabia, including resident and non-resident Agencies, is wellplaced to support the Kingdom in achieving its goals. Several key means of implementation 
have been identified. First is a focus onstrengthening policy implementation, institution 
building and systems developmentas a fundamental for strengthening capacity development in 
the country and a continuing prerequisite for sustainable development. This will be centred 
on development outcomes, proper management of human resources and adequate financial 
resources and tools to achieve CCSF results. 
The national capacity development paradigm that represents the heart of the United Nations’ 
mandate thus will be heavily emphasized, positioning Agencies well vis-a-vis the 
Government in support of the 2011 Busan Declaration on development cooperation. This 
gives tangible expression to national ownership, and enabling more informed choices and 
decisions at both organizational and individual levels. Capacity development also will be 
linked with Saudi Arabia‟s overall need for decentralization to address human development 
inequities, which will change the political, bureaucratic and institutional landscapes alike, 
underscoring balanced regional development. Decentralization of programme activities and 
services is critical because many of the country‟s most urgent issues are most pronounced in 8
less developed regions of the country. Complementarities, ability to “scale up” initiatives, 
and impact and cost effectiveness also will be taken into account. 
Likewise, promoting better distribution of development benefits to ensure social inclusion, 
especially for women and youth, in programming outcomes is imperative, given that 
inequities in access to delivery of quality services are often among the root causes of lower 
than expected human development results in some parts of the country. In all, this will 
involve more effective targeting of programme activities. An important opportunity 
specifically exists for the United Nations to build capacity for a human rights-based approach 
to development, specifically empowering vulnerable groups likereligious minorities, women, 
youth/children and migrant workers.
Finally, developing the capacity of the Government in obtaining, analyzing and utilizing 
quality data through improved and innovative knowledge management – employing new 
mechanisms and expanded access to regional and global United Nations expertise and 
databases – will be crucial to ensure sound policy decisions and effective programming 
results. 
These key means of implementation will be further refined during UNCCSF implementation 
through coordination mechanisms to be developed; some may require collaborative or joint 
programming or funding. Overall, they are expected to give rise to:
 Better United Nations-wide coordinated efforts with national institutions
 Better balance between policy development and effective service delivery 
 Better balance between development of the centre and local communities 
 Increasing empowerment of society to take active part in the development process
 Increasing commitment to social inclusion, particularly for vulnerable groups like 
minorities, women, youth, and migrant workers
 Stronger focus on results through monitoring and evaluation mechanisms
The results and activities to be undertaken by the United Nations are briefly described below. 
A Results Framework is detailed in Annex 1.9
Development Challenges
Key national strategies and policies point to the centrality of institutional governance 
capacities to sustaining the Kingdom‟s hard won development gains. In solidifying more 
effective and accountable governance and achieving progress on the rights agenda, the 
Government recognizes the need for capacity development at systemic, institutional and 
individual levels. Importance is to be given to not only individual skills but to embedding 
institutional attitudes and behaviours that emphasize principles of effective and accountable 
governance. 
Calls for more effective and accountable governance are on the rise, as are concerns for more 
regionally balanced and inclusive development taking into account the empowerment of 
vulnerable groups like religious minorities, women and migrant workers. While progress in 
governance capacities have been noted in recent years, important challenges remain, 
particularly with regards issues of transparency, accountability and participation, and rightsbased approaches to development.
The United Nations is committed to building partnerships in existing structures that can 
clarify roles and responsibilities for more effective development policies, decision-making 
and service delivery. Weseek to assist in creating social cohesion and preventing conflict 
horizontally between various regional groups and segments of society, and vertically, 
between the Government and citizens, both making governance more inclusive. 
On the horizontal perspective, needs exist to address regional imbalances in development 
results and improve institutional systems of administration in less developed regions. This 
includes enhancing monitoring and effectiveness of local Government, often at the frontline 
UNCCSF Result1: Effective & Accountable Governance 
Outcome 1.1: By 2016, national capacities for effective evidence-based policy 
making are enhanced towards socially inclusive development results. 
Outcome 1.2: By 2016, local capacities for social accountability 
strengthenedthrough access to information, participation and remedy in decisionmaking. 
Outcome 1.3: By 2016,capacities in Government and civil society enhancedto 
address human rights and access to justice, particularly for vulnerable groups. 
National Development Plan Priorities: Institutional and administrative development, 
including improved organizational effectiveness and efficiency, enhanced transparency 
and accountability; balanced regional development; enhanced national unity and security; 
guarantee human rights; promote of a culture of performance excellence; ensure 
consistency between institutional structures and mandates of these agencies.
Relevant MDGs: MDG1: Eradicate extreme poverty; MDG3: Promote gender equality.10
of development challenges and results. Enhanced systems of local governance respecting 
rights based approaches also can significantly reinforce stability through further enhancing 
local participation in decision-making processes.
With regards the vertical sphere, a need also exists to address social exclusion and improve 
protection of religious minorities, women and migrant workers. Civil society is an 
indispensable partner for achieving national development goals, with new NGOs arising to 
convey the voice of the public and specific segments ofsociety through peaceful social 
dialogue. An increasingly vocal and social media savvy youth, are now engaged in greater 
public participation and debates over the future of development- with women often at the 
helm. To engage these trends a series of new measures are in need to engage the voice and 
aspirations of society. 
UNCT Responses
Outcome 1.1: By 2016, national capacities for effective evidence-based policy making
are enhanced towards socially inclusive development results. 
The UN willsupport partners in development of a series of analytic reviews on ways to 
achieve more socially inclusive and regionally-balanced development results. This will feed 
into the implementation of the 9th National Development Planand its monitoring. Support will 
also be provided to analyse post-2015 development frameworks to be more focused on 
socially inclusive and regionally-balanced development results. 
Emphasizing a human development approach, the United Nations will support efforts to 
ensure that key Ministries are better enabled to meet their policy goals and to formulate 
rights-based economic and development policies that address issues of religious minorities, 
women and the poor. In particular the UN will support a National Rural Development 
Strategy to address inter-linkages and inequities between urban and peri-urban areas. 
Likewise, capacity development will accord special emphasis on women‟s skills and 
participation in policy decision-making and development policy. 
The UN will also support design of National and Local Human Development Reports and 
National MDG Reports, as well as capacity support given for statistical systems and 
monitoring and evaluation of implementation of the Ninth NDP. Policy advice also will be 
offered to development of the next NDP and related policies. The UN will also support 
training on development effectiveness and results based management as well asdevelopment 
of new indicators on sustainable and inclusive development. 
Cooperation will also place special emphasis on pursuing an agenda of social empowerment. 
This will include research on application of the UN‟s new Multi-Dimensional Poverty Index 
(MPI) through new strategies and policies for poverty reduction, research on social subsidy 
reforms, and ways to enhance social safety nets for the vulnerable in society.A trend toward 
social empowerment, as opposed to social welfare, will be encouraged, including initiatives 
in policy and advocacy work on rights-based approaches and poverty reduction which 
remains a serious issue among the citizenry. 11
Outcome 1.2: By 2016, local capacities for social accountability arestrengthenedthrough 
improvedaccess to information, participation and remedy in decision-making. 
Calls have arisen for enhancing the representational nature of the country‟s systems of 
governance. Scope exists for enhancing the state of the electoral process; political inclusion 
and integration require creating an interest in the political system for excluded or vulnerable 
groups, particularly women. Most women still have very limited roles in public decision 
making, which undermines their access to development decision-making and impedes 
expression of opinions and social accountability through legislative channels. 
Based on passage in 2011 of new national policy on allowing women to stand as candidates 
and vote in the 2015 municipal elections, and a new law on municipal elections, the UN will 
provide technical assistance to the 2015 elections, bringing in best practice from our global 
electoral assistance experiences and on ways to engage women and related NGOs in the 
political process. Support will also be explored to support post-electoral legislative capacity 
development assistance to the national and local legislative bodies.
Local capacities for engaging social accountability trends also have to do with enhanced 
capacities in local public administration, through which most development policies and plans 
get implemented. To this end, the UN will also support launch of a new Urban Observatory 
Network among local partners across the country, to support improved access to information, 
transparency and participation of citizens in local governance. This will also support regional 
networking, facilitation of partnerships and knowledge exchange, including for strategic 
urban planning. 
The United Nations as a whole has several comparative advantages in supporting Saudi 
Arabia to effectively engage systems of transparency, accountability and participation in 
governance. In addition to the UN‟s global normative processes, operational activities of all 
Agencies emphasize that development and fundamental freedoms are interdependent and 
mutually reinforcing. In particular, the United Nations‟ capacity development paradigm 
proves useful to address opportunities for institutional change, leadership and empowerment.
Outcome 1.3: By 2016,capacities in Government and civil society enhancedto address 
human rights and access to justice, particularly for vulnerable groups
The UN‟simpartiality and track record in advocating a rights-based approach complements
and enrichesthe focus of cooperation above. This entails advocacy for adherence to 
international standards and mobilization of global best practices in rights-based policy 
making and institutional capacity development within Government and civil society. 
Building on its membership in the UN Human Rights Council 2011-12 term, Saudi Arabia is 
also planning measures to improve the situation of vulnerable groups within the country, 
including religious minorities, women and foreign workers. Along with other Gulf countries
the Kingdom provided a constructive role in 2011 passage of the new UN Convention on 
Domestic Workers while in 2012 Saudi Arabia issued new draft legislation which if passed in 
coming years could see an end to the individual sponsorship and passport control systems for 
migrant workers. New legislation to combat human trafficking has also been issued in recent 
years with a need for effective implementation capacities. The UN will engage in dialogues 
with national institutions to support progress on these fronts and seek to initiate capacity 
development activities. Examples could include capacity development for National Human 12
Rights Institutions as well as cooperation with key Ministries for adherence to international 
labour standards. The UN will also explore cooperation with entities on expanding access to 
justice, based on the new Government blueprints for judicial reform in recent years.
With regards civil society capacity development and women‟s empowerment, the UN will 
support capacity development for a group of new civil society organizations and foundations 
created in recent years. This will includesupport to institutional capacities of the Prince 
Sultan Development Fund for Women Empowerment to carry out its household and NGO
grant assistance programmes within the country, the Al Anoud Foundation Youth Center
focused on engaging volunteerism within the Kingdom for achieving development goals, and 
the Al Ghad Youth Forum focused on dialogues and social media to channel the voice and 
aspirations of the new generation to the Government. 
National implementing partners: Ministry of Economy and Planning, Ministry of Municipal 
& Rural Affairs, Ministry of Justice, Ministry of Labour, National Commission for Human 
Rights, Saudi Human Rights Society, Prince Sultan Development Fund for Women, the Al 
Anoud Foundation YouthCenter,Al Ghad Youth Forum.
UNCT roles: UNDP serves as lead agency in the UNCT for this pillar of the CCSF, with a 
tentative resource allocation of $15million (2012-16), all of which is expected as Government 
cost-sharing from national partners under specific projects. Partner UN agencies are expected 
to include UNDESA, OHCHR, UN Women and ILO. 13
Development Challenges
While Saudi Arabia is the Arab region‟s largest economy and has seen positive GDP growth, 
reaching a record 6.8% GDP growth rate in 2011 and seeing record oil export revenues in 
recent years, it is the diversification and inclusiveness of such growth that will determine the
sustainability of the Kingdom‟s aspired emergence as a major economy. 
Diversification of the economy beyond oil has been a topic of attention for decades, but oil 
exports still make up 90% of public revenues today. Meanwhile, although a high income 
country, poverty still persists particularly in less developed regions of the country where 
national GDP growth has not always seen results. Improving standards of living for less 
developed parts ofthe Kingdom remains a challenge. Overall, the impact that growth can 
have on reducing inequalityis conditioned by a variety of factors, including the sectoral 
pattern of output, the elasticity of employment, and prevailing levels of inter-regional 
inequities. A priority isthus to ensure that growth can be of greater benefit to all, including 
the less developed regions of the country. 
This is exacerbated by a youth bulge nation-wide with young males and females making up 
60% of the population. Saudi youth face 30% unemployment and are often resigned to public 
sector posts, while expatriates enjoy 90% of all jobs within a dynamic and growing private 
sector, with most earnings repatriated abroad. The quota based affirmative action policies of 
the past (termed „Saudization‟) have had challenges in increasing the share of locals in the 
workforce. New efforts at growth-oriented employment creation and human capacity 
development are in focus, so the youth can effectively compete with expatriates and more 
fully participate in national economic prosperity.
In particular, women are seriously under-represented in the labour force, comprising only 
12.8 percent of total Saudi employment and experiencing unemployment levels four times 
greater than those for Saudi men. Saudi youth, male and female, thus represent a missed
opportunity to harness the vast human capital of the Kingdom.Economic development 
UNCCSF Result2: Inclusive Growth and Employment
Outcome 2.1: By 2016, a more sectorally and geographically diversified economy, 
with expansion of non-oil industry and employment opportunities
Outcome 2.2: By 2016, a more fair and competitive labour market, with focus on 
youth and women competitive capacities and status of migrant workers
National Development Plan Priorities: Diversify the economic base; ensure 
institutional and spatial diversification; diversify exports and Government revenues; 
continue to improve living standards and quality of life; develop national labour force; 
support a knowledge economy; enhance competitiveness of the national economy; 
develop the Small and Medium Enterprise sector.
Relevant MDGs:MDG 1: Eradicate poverty; MDG 8: Develop a global partnership for 
development14
policies and approaches need to change to generate more productive employment and 
improve labour market outcomes as well as labour productivity.
To address these imbalances, it will be critical for the Kingdom to reinvest the ongoing oil 
boom wealth to rapidly expand non-oil industrial sectors and thereby set the foundations for a 
shift from the oil-export based welfare state of the past to a more market-based competitive 
economy of the future. Some of the building blocks and already in place and progress is 
being seen in some non-oil sectors. But much more concerted efforts are needed and a special 
focus is needed on youth and women to support the generation of competencies to effectively 
compete for future jobs. It will also be critical to ensure efficient infrastructure with a wave 
of new construction projects underway in this regard. Likewise, improving national 
competitive capacities through technological progress, including through enhanced ICT 
capacities will be vital. 
UNCT Responses
Outcome 2.1: By 2016, a more sectorally and geographically diversified economy with 
expansion of non-oil industry and employmentopportunities
The comparative advantage of the United Nations with regard to this pillar stems from its 
neutrality and its positive working relationship with the Government, as well as its global 
knowledge base. This includes rich experience in economic diversification, addressing 
regional imbalances, employment promotion initiatives and improved infrastructure.
In particular, the United Nations will provide policy advice to undertake macro-economic 
forecasts of global and local oil markets and prices and risks to over-reliance on oil exports 
for future GDP growth, reforms of core macro-economic policies and subsidy systems, new 
trade and investment capacities, and ways to further diversify the economy beyond oil 
exports. This will include strategies for key employment generating sectors with a focus on 
knowledge economy. 
The UN will provide specific support for expanding non-oil sectors like travel and tourism 
and the IT sector. The UN will also help design and implement a new National Spatial 
Strategy to address regional diversification of growth and development results, with a special 
focus on less developed regions of the country, and will support sustainability of air, sea and 
road transport and infrastructure, including low-carbon approaches. Advisory support 
likewise will also be offered for overall trade and investment policy; design of new labour 
market policies; capacity development for technical/vocational education and training 
systems; and promotion of small and medium enterprises. 
Outcome 2.2: By 2016, a more fair and competitive labour market, with focus on youth 
and women competitive capacities and status of migrant workers
The UN will support review of labour policiesand challenges for expanding youth and 
women competitive capacities and addressing status of migrant labour. A special focus will 
also be explored with partners on Decent Work agenda. A new National Youth Strategy will 
be designed and launched to address integrated challenges of employment generation and 
educational competency generation. Making use of the UN‟s global reach and presence on

Development Challenges
Attainment of the highest standard of education, health, nutrition, water, sanitation and 
hygiene, and social welfare services are fundamental rights. Yet although many of the 
Kingdom‟s key human development indicators have improved since the establishment of the 
State, significant disparities exist between regions and between rural and urban areas, even as 
the capacity of local governments to deliver services and provide the necessary infrastructure 
is limited. Gender inequality in social services remains a barrier to social justice and 
development, while youth are having access to resources, they are often confronted with adult 
issues 
For improved social inclusion and equity, interlinked strategic challenges will need to be 
addressed, including access and availability, and overcoming geographical barriers.
Administrative barriers encompass a need for strengthened attention to vulnerable groups and 
rural areas, as well as insufficient budget allocations. The role of non-State actors in the 
sector remains highly underdeveloped. As such, issues of inequality in relation to social protection 
and social services can be addressed; and the support provided work done on unemployment benefits, 
pension schemes can be included. 
Challenges in achieving quality education are particularly crucial given Saudi Arabia‟s young 
population and its national ambitions. Key issues here are particularly focused on the quality 
of education, and with remedies for skills mismatches with the labour market. Ongoing 
development remains critical to keep pace with advancements in various fields, as well as to 
ensure development of a knowledge-based national economy and enhanced national 
competitiveness in an integrated global economy. A low level of preschool education, as well 
as persistent issues of dropouts, repetition and illiteracy, also must be addressed.

people.

Enhance human development, expand the range of options open to individuals to enable 
them to acquire and use knowledge skills and expertise, and provide equitably

For its part, the health sector confronts important and complex challenges to improve health 
outcomes; this includes not only continued expansion of services, but also particularly 
encompasses implementation of policies and mechanisms for structural transformation of the 
health system. Special emphasis will be given to expanding awareness among youth of their 
right to health, including reproductive health. There is a need to strengthen capacity of the 
health sector for planning and delivery of quality health care and prevention services. 
KSA is increasingly involved in response to HIV at the regional level, and they are at the 
forefront of the Arab Strategy on AIDS (in partnership with UNAIDS). However, it seems to 
fall short of implementing its own national commitments. There is a complete lack of 
surveillance data on most-at-risk-populations (Sex workers, Men having Sex with Men, and 
IDUs). It would be useful for the UN to support national partners to conduct surveillance on 
MARPs in order to have a better understanding of the epidemic among these groups..
Lastly, despite the existence of the welfare state, sustainability of its outcomes remains a 
critical challenge. More targeted social protection services need to be made available to 
address the needs of the poorest and most vulnerable. Numerous rights and empowerment 
issues also remain to be addressed, including issues of juvenile justice, ofvarious forms of 
abuse, violence and neglect, such as trafficking, with regard to refugees.
Outcome 1 Saudi Arabia has institutionalised improved social protection and poverty

United Nations concerns under this pillar thus will focus on strengthening policies and 
supporting the translation of them into delivery of integrated, quality education, health, 
nutrition, water/sanitation and social protection services at district, community and family

emphasized, as will inter-sectoral collaboration, particularly at middle management level. 
Capacity development will include areas such as standardization of practices, improvement of 
planning and budgeting, and human resource management, with a systematic approach to 
monitoring and evaluation institutionalized. 
The UNCT‟s comparative advantages lie largely in its core mandate of basic social services; 
its strong links to global expertise and international best practices; its commitment to help the 
Government achieve national goals; and its relationship of trust with relevant Ministries. The 
United Nations will work to ensure that decision makers are better able to develop and 
deliver health, education and protection services as well as sustain processes of 
empowerment for women and youth in the economic and public life. 
Outcome 2 Saudi Arabia is providing equitable delivery of quality social services for all 
people. 
In so doing, the UNCT will capitalize on its comparative advantages in promoting livelihoods 
and life skills to bring countries to par with international standards, as well as in fostering 
social dialogue toward the formulation of comprehensive gender-sensitive and child-friendly 
social policies. Life-cycle investment planning to promote child-friendly and gender-sensitive 18
budget development represents a key opportunity. Critically, the United Nations‟ comparative 
advantages on related issues such as public administration reform and community 
empowerment offer cross-cutting relevance to the social sectors as well.

Development Challenges
While holding the world‟s largest oil reserve, the Kingdom has also seen one of the world‟s 
fastest growth rates in local energy consumption in recent years, now surpassing the GDP 
growth rate. This has caused concern among various entities in Government as to the future 
longevity of the nation‟s reserves and the lost opportunity to oil export revenues from 
increased local diversion. As a result, a new set of policy goals are being pursued to expand 
energy efficiency and renewable energy in the Kingdom in order to conserve oil for future 
export revenues while also reducing its carbon footprint. 
Despite this ambitious agenda for change, capacities for sustainable use of energy remain 
weak, confronting a long-standing and entrenched system of oil burning power generation 
and heavily subsidized energy use. New policies and regulatory frameworks are thus needed 
to support a transformational change towards clean energy use. In addition a need exists for 
enhanced human capacities in government and business, while innovative partnerships 
among public entities and between public and private partners are also needed. 
Furthermore, tipping points exist with regard to natural resources such as arable land and 
freshwater both of which are very scarce in the Kingdom.Risks of unsustainable policies and 
practices include reduced agricultural productivity, heightened water scarcity, increased 
exposure to extreme weather and flood events, collapse of ecosystems, increased health risks, 
and increased economic and social vulnerability, all of which could imperil gains toward 
achievement of development goals. Already, urbanization and industrialization, high density 
of land, sea and air transport, and increased volume of waste of all types have increased the 
country‟s pollution levels, negatively affecting various ecosystem services and indicators. 
Use of groundwater to meet growing urban demand has had serious implications in terms of 
rising water salinity, falling water reserves, and increased soil degradation and soil salinity; in 
addition, desertification and soil erosion represents a major challenge, caused by increased 
population activity, overgrazing, expansion of agriculture and cities, coupled with a lack of 
rain and vulnerability to recurrent droughts. Further highlighting the strategic role of

Development Challenges
The Busan Partnership for Effective Development Cooperation was launched in 2011 
with partners including Saudi Arabia agreeing to establish a Global Partnership for Effective 
Development Cooperation. This declaration for the first time establishes an agreed 
framework for development cooperation that embraces traditional OECD donors, SouthSouth partners, the emerging BRICS economies, CSOs and private sector foundations. This is 
seen by many as marking a turning point for international development cooperation, with the 
growing role of Southern providers of ODA of increasing relevance to development trends. 
Among these, Saudi Arabia holds a special place, as the largest Southern provider of ODA. 
As noted under the MDG8 component of the 2011 National MDG Report, developed 
with UN assistance, since 1973, the Kingdom has provided over $100 billion of ODA to over 
83 countries, with a major focus on cooperation with North Africa, Sub-Saharan Africa and 
Asia. About 5% of this amount is through multilateral channels like the UN. For example, in 
2010-11 Saudi Arabia contributed $183 million to UN relief efforts in Somalia, Haiti and
Pakistan. 
Meanwhile, Saudi Arabia is also expanding its role in global political and economic 
decision-making fora, from dialogues around the post-2015 Development Framework, to the 
the G20 Development Working Group. Saudi Arabia has also played an important role 
convening global dialogues on dialogue among civilizations and has supported various UN 
initiatives in recent years including serving as a founding member of the new UN CounterTerrorism Center, becoming a UN Human Rights Council member for the 2011-12 term, and 
is in process to possibly secure its first ever seat on the UN Security Council for the 2014-16 
term.

IV. Implementation
Throughout implementation of the UNCCSF, the UNCT will focus on the most vulnerable 
groups in society, with explicit provisions for ensuring their active and effective participation 
in decision making. To contribute to the reduction of rural-urban and regional disparities that 
underlie much of the challenges to equity and social cohesion in Saudi Arabia, the United 
Nations will target poor rural areas and specific impoverished groups. Particular importance 
will be given to effective links between the State and civil society. 
The UNCT and United Nations Resident Coordinator will be responsible for the effectiveness 
of United Nations activities. These arrangements will support progress toward the use of 
national systems for implementation, management and monitoring, based on internationally 
recognized standards and good practices. The UNCT will discuss and determine which 
outputs can be implemented within inter-agency Joint UN Programmes. 
Relevant UN Theme Groups will be established by the UNCT to help it monitor the 
UNCCSF [see also Section V]. The UN Theme Group on South-South Cooperation and 
Global Partnership is one example. UNTG workplans on collaborative activities will be 
developed with clear goals and objectives, to be integrated into the Annual Report and 
Workplan of the Office of the Resident Coordinator. Regional cooperation also will be 
supported and encouraged with the Government, particularly in discussions on commitments 
to international treaties and United Nations instruments.
Provisions of the UNCCSF will be implemented through individual UN agency Country 
Cooperation Frameworks and Country Programmes as agreed separately with relevant 
partners in the Kingdom. Selection and definition of individual agencies‟ goals, outcomes and 
strategies will seek to be consistent with the UNCCSF. Individual UN agency Country 
Cooperation Frameworks and Country Programmes should also specify how they contribute 
to UNCCSF objectives and cooperation strategies.
V. Monitoring and Evaluation
A set of objectively verifiable and repeatable key performance indicators is essential for 
monitoring, evaluating and reporting on achievement. Key indicators, accompanied by 
baselines and targets, have been formulated for each Outcome under each of the four pillars 
of cooperation. To refine baselines and further refine programme strategies, several surveys 
will be undertaken during the UNCCSF cycle. [See the Results Matrices in Annex 1 for 
comprehensive monitoring and evaluation indicators to be used.] At the same time, because 
development is a process, the UNCCSF may have to be adapted to respond to changes in 
Saudi Arabia‟s economic, political or social situations.
The UNCT will meet quarterly and produce brief quarterly reports on progress in 
implementation as well as opportunities and constraints still faced. Government and partner 
representatives will be invited during the year to provide strategic guidance. This overall 
monitoring and evaluation plan will particularly show its value during UNCCSF Annual 
Review Meetings, which will serve as the basis for tracking and reporting on UNCT 
performance. Annual Reviews will validate conclusions, including lessons learnt and best 
practices, which should feed into policy advocacy and preparation of new Annual Work 25
Plans. The Annual Reviews also may provide important inputs for Annual Reports for 
individual Agencies, the Resident Coordinator and donors, as well as data and analysis for the 
final UNCCSF Evaluation, and may reflect on issues such as development effectiveness and 
joint resource mobilization. A mid-term evaluation by end-2014will be conducted by the 
Office of the Resident Coordinator, synchronized as much as possible with respective 
Agencies‟ Country Programme mid-term reviews. This will be undertaken with the objective 
of obtaining substantive feedback on progress toward stated Outcomes under each pillar.
The mid-term review will focus on (1) whether the UNCCSF has made the best use of the 
United Nations‟ comparative advantages in Saudi Arabia; (2) the coherence of the Agencies‟ 
contribution toward achieving national priorities; (3) whether the UNCCSF has helped 
achieve the selected priorities in the national development framework; and (4) impact of 
capacity development initiatives. In all, this will provide the opportunity for any mid-course 
adjustments to ensure that United Nations efforts 2012-2016 remain focused on the 
Kingdom‟s national priorities. In addition, achievements, lessons learnt and best practices 
will be disseminated, as will constraints encountered, to inform the design of the next 
UNCCSF in the post-2015 context. 26
